sow.alignment: Directly targets the SoW evidence and graph outcome. Covers pentadactyl-limb reasoning and data interpretation relevant to Topic 4. This exemplar does not replace separate teaching of named human fossils, stone tools, classification or natural-selection mechanisms.

safety: Paper and screen lesson; no live organisms, biological cultures or chemical work.
practicalAlternative: All evidence is supplied for offline use. Discuss, point, annotate or dictate instead of cutting cards or writing extended prose.

access.supported: Same scientific objective, with chunked cards, word bank, read-aloud access and short evidence stems. Accept accurately explained oral or annotated responses.
access.standard: Use two evidence sources and a reasoned explanation independently.
access.stretch: Evaluate limitations, explain a mechanism and transfer to unfamiliar evidence.
access.regulation: Offer solo or partner working and a quiet response route. Preview the sequence; allow a brief reset and re-entry at the next numbered task. No compulsory performance or timed competition.

title: Evolution: build the evidence case
subtitle: A museum investigation using fossils, limb anatomy and DNA
objective: Interpret fossil, anatomical and DNA evidence to justify a claim about evolution and state a limitation.
priorLearning: DNA carries inherited information; species show inherited variation.
Natural selection can change inherited characteristics in populations over generations.
Read a horizontal bar chart and compare numbers.
success: Identify what an evidence source actually shows.
Use two different evidence types to explain shared ancestry or change over time.
Read the DNA graph accurately and avoid claiming that one living species changed into another.

vocabulary.meaning: Change in inherited characteristics of populations over generations.
Preserved remains or traces of past organisms.
An ancestral population shared by two or more descendant groups.
Having a shared evolutionary origin, even when function differs.
An explanation supported by evidence and reasoning.
A reason the evidence cannot answer every part of a question.

equipment: Projector or offline HTML/PPTX; pupil evidence sheet and selected response page.
preparation: Print evidence page for each pupil or pair; select one response route after retrieval.
Keep the answers separate. Pre-teach Ma = million years ago and that a larger Ma value is older.
Explain that Q/A/B/C DNA values are invented practice data; real fossil ages and features are sourced summaries.

misconceptions.claim: Whales evolved from living humans because both have limb bones.
misconceptions.correction: The shared arrangement supports shared ancestry; neither living group is presented as the ancestor of the other.
misconceptions.check: Ask pupils to replace the direct arrow between living tips with branches from an ancestor.

misconceptions.claim: One fossil proves the exact whole evolutionary route.
misconceptions.correction: Dated fossils and other evidence are combined; preservation and discovery are incomplete.
misconceptions.check: Ask what a fossil skeleton cannot show about all earlier populations.

misconceptions.claim: A bar of 24 means 24% of every gene is different.
misconceptions.correction: The graph compares only 100 selected aligned DNA positions in fictional species.
misconceptions.check: Ask pupils to name the sampled quantity before describing the bar.

slides.title: A whale has finger bones. Why?
body: Today: use evidence to write a museum caption.
You may explain by speaking, writing or annotating.
slides.notes: Invite one prediction without judging confidence. Say: 'Our job is to connect what we can observe with what it can reasonably tell us.' Share the objective; offer solo or partner route. Do not collect family or personal ancestry examples.

slides.title: Retrieve the tools
body: R1. What carries inherited information?
R2. Does evolution describe change in one animal during its life, or populations over generations?
R3. Which is older: 50 Ma or 33 Ma?
slides.notes: Allow 30 seconds quiet thought, then simultaneous responses. R1 DNA; genes are sections of DNA. R2 populations over generations. R3 50 Ma, because it means 50 million years before today. If two or more errors, read the vocabulary and model R3 on a number line before continuing.

slides.title: Read fossils as evidence
body: A dated fossil records a past combination of traits.
Compare the legs and flippers through time.
This timeline does not prove a direct ancestor chain.
slides.notes: Teacher think-aloud: 'I first read the ages. Pakicetus is older than Dorudon. I next compare the features: walking limbs versus flippers and tiny hind limbs. Together, dated fossils support change in whale relatives through time. I cannot say every fossil species was a direct ancestor.' Ages are approximate ranges summarised from the NHM. The visual simplifies morphology and is not a skeletal reconstruction.

visual.title: Whale relatives through deep time
visual.description: Simplified timeline of three extinct whale relatives using Natural History Museum approximate ages. Separate branches are not drawn: the timeline orders evidence and does not claim a direct ancestor sequence.

elements.text: Fossils reveal different combinations of traits

About 50 Ma
Four walking legs
Whale-group

Movement in water
and on land

slides.title: The same underlying plan
body: Compare corresponding bones, not just the outline.
The inherited pattern can serve different functions.
Shared origin is a stronger claim than “they look alike”.
slides.notes: Point in order to one upper bone, two lower bones, wrist and five digits on both limbs. Say: 'I can explain the correspondence as inheritance from a shared ancestor, followed by modification in different lineages.' Five digits is the ancestral pentadactyl pattern; not every living whale species retains the same visible digit count. The chosen schematic represents a five-digit flipper and does not show every small bone or realistic proportions.

visual.title: One inherited limb pattern, different functions
visual.description: Schematic human forelimb and a five-digit whale flipper: one upper limb bone, two lower limb bones, wrist bones and five digits. Bone proportions and numbers of small wrist and digit bones are simplified; colours link corresponding regions, not exact scale.

elements.text: Same bone plan; different shapes. Not to scale.

slides.title: Read the DNA graph carefully
body: Name the quantity before making a claim.
Q and A differ at 2 of the 100 sampled positions.
This supports closer relatedness than Q and C.
slides.notes: Model: 'The x-axis measures differences, so a shorter bar means greater similarity. Q/A has 2 differences; Q/C has 24. For corresponding DNA this supports Q/A sharing a more recent ancestor. It does not identify the ancestor or date a split.' State clearly: these are constructed sample data, not measurements from real species.

visual.title: Read the genetic evidence
visual.description: Constructed practice data for fictional species. A differs from Q at 2 of 100 aligned DNA positions, B at 11 and C at 24. Fewer differences support closer relatedness for comparable DNA; this short sample alone cannot establish a complete tree.

elements.text: Constructed sample data: DNA compared with Q
Differences in the same aligned 100 DNA positions

slides.title: Evolution branches
body: Living species sit at the tips.
A shared ancestor sits at a branch point.
No living tip is labelled “more evolved”.
slides.notes: Shares the preceding 3-minute I do stage. Briefly trace the two Q/A branches backwards to their nearest shared point. Say: 'This is one possible model; these comparisons support Q/A closeness but do not establish the B/C branching order. Scientists compare all pairs, much more DNA and other evidence.' Do not infer time from branch length.

visual.title: Branching does not mean a ladder
visual.description: One possible schematic hypothesis for fictional Q, A, B and C. The Q-only comparisons support Q/A closeness but do not establish the B/C branching order. Branch lengths do not show measured time.

elements.text:
Tips = living species in this model
Branch lengths are not a time scale.

Q did not
evolve from
living A.

slides.title: Museum label rescue
body: W1. Read the claim and choose: keep, edit or reject.
“Whales came from living humans because both have similar finger-bone patterns.”
Use Evidence A and F on your card sheet.
slides.notes: Run a reasoning clinic: 1 minute private decision; 2 minutes pair or teacher comparison; 2 minutes edit; 2 minutes test the edit against evidence. Accept spoken or written verdicts. Correct verdict: edit/reject the direct-ancestry claim, retain that homologous limb organisation supports a shared ancestor. Dated fossil relatives provide independent evidence of changing limbs. Ask: 'Which precise words go beyond the evidence?'
slides.prompt: Which part is an observation, and which part is an unjustified inference?

slides.title: A second label arrives
body: W2. “Q and A are identical. The graph proves A became Q.”
Use the DNA card to repair both errors.
W3. Why use more than one evidence type?
slides.notes: Shares the preceding 7-minute We do stage. Q/A have two sampled differences and do not have identical sampled DNA. Fewer differences support a closer relationship; not descent of one living species from another. Independent sources can strengthen a claim and reveal weaknesses in any one source. Model a concise repaired label after pupils offer alternatives.
slides.reveal: Q and A are most similar in this sample. This supports a recent shared ancestor; it does not prove A became Q.

slides.title: Which claim is best supported?
body: The sample has 2 Q/A differences and 24 Q/C differences.
Choose a claim and be ready to explain one word.
slides.notes: All pupils answer privately before discussion. If B is not secure, circle the sampled quantity and trace the shared branch point again. Challenge 'prove' language. Then release to the suitable independent route.

options.text: Q evolved directly from living A.
options.feedback: A living tip is not identified as the ancestor of Q.

options.text: Q and A probably share a more recent ancestor than Q and C.
options.feedback: Fewer differences in corresponding DNA support this relationship, with the sample limitation.

options.text: Q and C share no ancestor.
options.feedback: More differences do not mean no shared ancestry.

options.text: A and Q have identical genomes.
options.feedback: They differ at two sampled positions, and whole genomes were not compared.

slides.title: Create the museum evidence panel
body: Choose Supported, Standard or Stretch with your teacher.
Explain a claim using two evidence types.
Include one number and one limitation.
slides.notes: Set a genuine product: a visitor should leave understanding why evidence supports evolution, without a false direct-ancestor claim. Pupils use the shared evidence page plus one route. At minute 4, check one observation and one inference; at minute 8, check the number and limitation. Do not require all three routes.

slides.title: A useful explanation structure
body: The evidence shows …
This supports … because …
It cannot tell us …
slides.notes: Shares the 11-minute independent stage. Supported route may dictate each sentence while the adult records exactly what was said. Standard pupils choose fossil + anatomical evidence and interpret the graph. Stretch pupils critique the two claims and propose the next investigation.

slides.title: Check your scientific decisions
body: Have you named an actual feature or number?
Have you explained how it supports the claim?
Have you avoided a claim the evidence cannot test?
slides.notes: Shares the 11-minute independent stage. Confer with pupils who have given generic 'they look alike' responses: ask them to locate one upper/two lower bones and describe correspondence. For advanced pupils ask whether the short DNA segment samples the whole genome.

slides.title: Compare, improve, hear the response
body: Share one evidence sentence in your chosen way.
Hear one helpful question.
Revise one claim that was too strong.
slides.notes: Use a light Lundy loop: provide space for all modes, voice by choice, audience through teacher or partner reading, influence through one recorded revision. Example feedback: 'You identified the same bone plan. Add shared ancestor rather than one living animal becoming another.' Show one strong response from the answer key without naming a pupil.

slides.title: What counts as a strong panel?
body: Accurate observation plus explained inference.
A number with its sampled quantity.
A specific limit on the conclusion.
slides.notes: Shares the preceding 3-minute review. Teacher-authored formative criteria: award one check for each of the three features, not an examination grade. A pupil can demonstrate all three orally or through annotations.

slides.title: One precise final claim
body: E1. Which species is closest to Q in the sample? Cite a number.
E2. Finish: a shared limb plan supports …
E3. Name one thing this evidence cannot establish.
slides.notes: A; 2 differences across 100 sampled DNA positions. Shared ancestry. It cannot establish a direct ancestor sequence, exact split time or full genome similarity from this sample. Collect the exit before the next lesson and reteach only the missing inference.

pupilPages.title: Shared evidence | Museum investigation
pupilPages.intro: Use this page with one response route. F and A are scientific summaries; D contains constructed sample data for fictional species.

cards.title: F | Fossils
cards.text: Pakicetus: about 50 million years ago, four walking legs. Ambulocetus: about 50–48 million years ago, large feet suited to movement in water. Dorudon: about 40–33 million years ago, flippers and very small hind legs. Approximate ages and broad features: Natural History Museum.

cards.title: A | Anatomical pattern
cards.text: A human forelimb and a five-digit whale flipper share corresponding regions: one upper bone, two lower bones, wrist bones and digits. Their shapes and functions differ. This shared arrangement is called homologous.

cards.title: D | Compare DNA
cards.text: Constructed sample data: the same aligned 100 DNA positions were compared in fictional species. Q/A differ at 2 positions; Q/B at 11; Q/C at 24. Scientists normally examine much more DNA and combine evidence.

cards.title: L | Evidence limits
cards.text: Fossilisation and discovery are incomplete. Similar body outlines can arise independently. One short DNA region is a sample. No card identifies an exact direct ancestor of a living species.

blocks.prompt: W1. Repair: “Whales came from living humans because both have similar finger-bone patterns.”
W2. Repair: “Q and A are identical. The graph proves A became Q.”
W3. Why combine different evidence types?

pupilPages.title: Supported route | Build a museum caption
pupilPages.intro: Keep the shared evidence page beside you. You may point, annotate or dictate. Words: shared ancestor • corresponding bones • fossil • sampled DNA • supports.

blocks.prompt: S1. Choose Pakicetus and Dorudon. Name one limb difference and say which is older.
S2. Complete: the human limb and whale flipper share … . This supports … .
S3. Constructed sample data above: which is most similar to Q? Use a number.
S4. Write a short visitor caption using one fossil fact and the limb pattern. Add one thing the evidence cannot tell us.

pupilPages.title: Standard route | Make a claim worth displaying
pupilPages.intro: Produce a visitor panel using the shared evidence. A drawing with an explanation is welcome.

blocks.prompt: M1. Compare Pakicetus and Dorudon using approximate age and one limb feature. Explain why this supports change over time.
M2. Explain why the corresponding human and whale limb bones support shared ancestry. Do not claim one living species became the other.
M3. Constructed sample data: Q/A = 2, Q/B = 11, Q/C = 24 differences in the same 100 positions. Identify the closest pair involving Q and justify it.
M4. Finish your panel with one specific limit and one additional piece of evidence you would seek.

pupilPages.title: Stretch route | Review the curator’s reasoning
pupilPages.intro: Critique the claims, then give the museum a better evidence statement.

blocks.text: Claim 1: “The three fossils prove a complete, direct chain to every modern whale.” Claim 2: “Q and A must have identical whole genomes because only two differences were counted.”

blocks.prompt: T1. Identify one error in each claim. Write corrected versions.
T2. Constructed sample data: a second aligned DNA region has Q/A = 4, Q/B = 14 and Q/C = 25 differences per 100 positions. Does it strengthen the same relationship? Explain, including a limitation.
T3. Design the next check: choose a new DNA region, a new fossil or a new anatomical feature. State a prediction and how the result could change confidence.
T4. Write a two-sentence visitor caption using at least two evidence types without claiming certainty about an exact ancestor.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection | Evidence before confidence
pupilPages.intro: Complete independently; short answers or a recorded oral explanation are enough.

blocks.prompt: E1. Constructed DNA sample: Q/A = 2, Q/B = 11, Q/C = 24 differences per 100 positions. Which comparison supports the closest relationship? Include the number.
E2. Finish: a shared limb plan supports … .
E3. Name one thing these evidence sources cannot establish.
L1. What question did your audience ask? How did it change or sharpen your caption?
My next useful step is…
choices: Explain shared ancestry with the limb diagram.

answers.label: R1–R3 retrieval
answers.answer: R1 DNA; genes are sections of DNA. R2 populations across generations, not an individual changing during its lifetime. R3 50 Ma is older than 33 Ma; Ma means million years ago.

answers.label: W1 museum label
answers.answer: Edit/reject the direct-ancestry claim. Observation: corresponding limb bones are present. Supported inference: shared ancestry, followed by modification of limb form and function. Humans are not presented as the ancestors of modern whales. Fossil relatives with different combinations of limb features support change through time.

answers.label: W2 DNA label
answers.answer: Q and A differ at 2 of the 100 sampled positions, so even this sample is not identical. Their greater similarity supports a recent shared ancestor compared with Q/C, not that living A became Q. Whole genomes were not measured.

answers.label: W3 combine evidence
answers.answer: Independent sources can agree on an explanation and compensate for limitations of a single source; fossil ages/features and corresponding anatomy offer different kinds of evidence. More evidence can also expose conflicts and prompt revision.

answers.label: Hinge A–D
answers.answer: B is best: fewer differences in corresponding sampled DNA support closer relatedness. A wrongly identifies a living species as the direct ancestor. C wrongly treats larger difference as no ancestry. D ignores two differences and extends a small sample to entire genomes.

answers.label: S1 / M1 fossil comparison
answers.answer: Pakicetus is older (about 50 Ma) and had walking legs; Dorudon is younger (about 40–33 Ma) with flippers and very small hind legs. Different limb combinations in dated relatives support evolutionary change through time. They do not on their own establish a direct ancestor chain.

answers.label: S2 / M2 anatomical reasoning
answers.answer: Corresponding one-upper/two-lower bone regions, wrist and digits suggest inherited organisation from a common ancestor, with forms modified in descendant lineages. They are homologous even though function differs. Accept a labelled diagram plus an accurate explanation.

answers.label: S3 / M3 graph
answers.answer: A is most similar to Q in the sample: 2 differences per 100 aligned positions, compared with 11 for B and 24 for C. Therefore Q/A is the closest supported pair involving Q. Do not generalise to identical entire genomes.

answers.label: S4 / M4 completed panel and next evidence
answers.answer: Model: “Older whale relatives had walking limbs, while later relatives such as Dorudon had flippers and tiny hind limbs. The shared arrangement of mammalian forelimb bones supports shared ancestry with modification. Fossils are incomplete and these examples do not prove the exact direct ancestor sequence.” For M4 accept comparing more corresponding DNA regions, analysing more dated fossil skeletons, or adding independent anatomical evidence with a stated purpose.

answers.label: T1 corrected claims
answers.answer: Claim 1 overstates completeness and direct descent: the fossil evidence supports change among whale relatives, but does not establish every ancestor or all branches. Claim 2 extends beyond a short sample and ignores two differences: Q/A are similar in those sampled positions; whole-genome identity is not shown.

answers.label: T2 second DNA region
answers.answer: Yes. Q/A again has the fewest differences (4 rather than 14 or 25), so a second region supports the same closest relationship. The two regions are still samples; evolutionary rates can differ and wider comparative evidence is needed. Do not calculate an exact divergence date.

answers.label: T3 next check
answers.answer: Accept a testable proposal, for example compare a third corresponding DNA region in Q/A/B/C; predict Q/A will be most similar; agreement raises confidence, disagreement requires examining sampling, alignment or the model. For fossils: seek more securely dated limb material and explain the expected pattern, allowing branches rather than a forced ladder.

answers.label: T4 integrated caption
answers.answer: Example: “Dated whale relatives show changes in limb form, and corresponding mammalian forelimb bones support shared ancestry. Similarity in comparable DNA provides another line of evidence, although fossil gaps and DNA sampling limit exact reconstructions.” Must integrate at least two types with no claim of a living direct ancestor.

answers.label: E1–E3 exit
answers.answer: E1 Q/A: 2 differences in 100 sampled aligned positions. E2 shared ancestry, followed by modification in descendant groups. E3 accept exact ancestors, an exact split date, complete fossil sequence, or whole genome similarity from 100 positions.

answers.label: L1 and next step
answers.answer: Answers vary; expect a specific question and an observable revision, such as replacing “proves” with “supports” or adding the sampled quantity. Act on the selected next step; do not grade confidence as knowledge.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes total: opening 2, retrieval 3, I do 10, We do 7, hinge 3, independent 11, review 3, exit 1. Zero-minute slides share their named stage allocation.

This is a focused Spring 1 evidence exemplar, not a complete Topic 4 course. Teach named human fossils, tools, classification and natural-selection examples elsewhere as required by the school sequence.

Keep fact, model and inference separate. The whale ages/features are sourced summaries. The limb drawing is an explanatory schematic. DNA numbers for Q/A/B/C are constructed sample data, designed for comparison rather than a real species claim.

Assessment: securely achieved when the pupil uses two specific observations, gives an accurate explanatory inference, reads one number with its sampled quantity and states a relevant limit. Oral and annotated evidence can meet the same criteria.

Reteach if necessary: cover all but two bars and read the x-axis aloud; then trace living tips backwards to a shared node. Avoid rewarding a long response that claims one modern species turned into another.
TA script: “Point to your observation. Now say what it supports. What would be too strong to claim?” Use 10 seconds processing time before offering the stem.
